sources.title: For him, or his? What la and jo reveal about my Kutchi
sources.citation: Farhan Abdulla, native-speaker East African Mombasa Kutchi research, October 2026 (Studies 008–011).
sources.notes: Speaker-supplied translations and judgments. Beneficiary and possession are attested for the cited constructions; a universal postposition analysis and the morphology of khade remain provisional. The source does not assign an individual study number to each sentence.

sources.title: Not just one way to say no: How negation works in my Kutchi
sources.citation: Farhan Abdulla, native-speaker East African Mombasa Kutchi research, October 2026 (Studies 008–011).
sources.notes: Speaker-supplied sentence forms and meanings. The two female-giver elicitation forms lack independently confirmed participant roles or full translations. Negative forms are recorded in their observed contexts, not as a predictive paradigm. The source does not assign an individual study number to each sentence.

glosses.definition_en: Marks a beneficiary in Hin la au(n) pe(n)sa kayose; also occurs in speaker-accepted food-related 'for' phrases.
glosses.note: Postposition is a provisional grammatical analysis. The food examples do not establish that beneficiary, purpose, payment and exchange uses are interchangeable.

entries.usage_note: Speaker attests Hin la, khadho la and khade la in the recorded constructions. Distribution outside these contexts remains untested.

glosses.definition_en: Links a possessor with what is possessed in Hin jo pe(n)sa and mujo bhaa jo ghar.
glosses.note: Preserve the older 'for' sense. Whether spaced Hin jo and written Hinjo have the same structure is unresolved.

glosses.gloss_en: negative element in an attested feminine-subject present clause
glosses.definition_en: Occurs in Nathi sume ('She is not sleeping'); also recorded in an untranslated female-giver elicitation form.
glosses.note: Do not assign the agreement controller or participant roles in hin ke au(n) pe(n)sa nathi dhya(n).

entries.usage_note: A complete negative agreement paradigm has not been established.

glosses.gloss_en: negative element in an attested desire clause
glosses.definition_en: Occurs with plural desired things in Mukhe hinee cheejeu(n) nathaa kape(n).
glosses.note: The grammatical feature controlling nathaa has not been confirmed.

entries.usage_note: Recorded with plural desired things; do not infer a universal plural-agreement rule.

expected_existing_glosses: negative element in an attested past construction

glosses.definition_en: Occurs before command forms in recorded prohibitions and before vendhose in a recorded future negative.
glosses.note: The contexts do not justify classifying nah as exclusively imperative.

expected_existing_glosses: negative existential element in an attested expression

glosses.gloss_en: negative element in attested giving constructions
glosses.definition_en: Occurs with dhine in the recorded past giving and permission examples; nai also occurs in an untranslated past-negative elicitation form.
glosses.note: Preserve the existing no-food sense. Nai is not established as exclusively past or existential.

glosses.definition_en: Recorded before bhaa in 'my brother' and before ghar in 'my house'.
glosses.note: Do not remove the older 'mine' gloss.

glosses.definition_en: Brother in Hee mujo bhaa jo ghar ai ('This is my brother's house').
Recorded in khadho la ('for the food') and in negative food constructions.
glosses.note: Exact speaker spelling is distinct from existing published khaadho. Whether the spellings denote one lexeme is unresolved.

entries.usage_note: Held for review because published khaadho also means food; do not silently merge near spellings.

glosses.definition_en: Form referring to food in the speaker-accepted phrase khade la ('for the food').
glosses.note: Whether khade is a separate headword, a form of khadho, or another relation remains unresolved.

entries.usage_note: Held for review; do not infer a khadho-to-khade case alternation from the two acceptable phrases.

glosses.definition_en: Command form recorded as 'Give!'; the source also records giving forms dye, dhine, dhineese, dhya(n) and dhinose.
glosses.note: The attested contexts do not establish a complete giving paradigm or feminine suffix analysis.

entries.usage_note: Grouping the recorded giving forms under de for search is a provisional lemma analysis; unelicited forms must not be generated.

glosses.definition_en: Permission or approval in the speaker's father's-permission sentence.
glosses.note: Exact raja is distinct from published rajaa ('approval'); do not normalize or merge without review. No 'king' meaning is supplied here.

entries.usage_note: Held for review because of a near-spelling collision with published rajaa.

forms.note: Occurs in Hee mukhe pe(n)sa natho dye, translated as a present negative. Do not assign an unconfirmed agreement feature to the giving form.
Occurs in recorded past-negative giving and permission sentences; no full paradigm inferred.
Past-negative female-giver elicitation; giver and recipient roles, agreement controller and full translation are unresolved.
Present-negative female-giver elicitation; giver and recipient roles, agreement controller and full translation are unresolved.
Occurs in the food-and-money account translated 'I gave a man food'; no further agreement features assigned.

examples.english_translation: I picked up money for him.
examples.note: Beneficiary reading of Hin la in the speaker's paired translation; ownership of the money is not asserted.
Possessive reading of spaced Hin jo; relationship to written Hinjo is untested.

examples.english_translation: for the food, I am taking it.
examples.note: Food-related 'for' reading; beneficiary, purpose, exchange and payment are not claimed interchangeable.

examples.kutchi_text: Au(n) hikro maru ke khadho dhinose. Hoo maru mukhe pe(n)sa dhine, khade la.
examples.english_translation: I gave a man food. That man gave me money for the food.
examples.note: Ke marks the food recipient in the first sentence; khade la is food-related in the second. The two sentences are kept together as supplied.

review_notes: The paired la/jo examples differ in phrase order; they do not establish a simple particle-swap test or general interchangeability.
Keep spaced Hin jo and written Hinjo distinct until a speaker confirms their relationship.
The added possessive jo and attributive mujo senses describe the recorded contexts; whether they are polysemy or separate homographs relative to older glosses remains to be reviewed.
Hin in the new paired translations refers to him/a possessor, while an existing published hin has a 'this' gloss. Do not attach a new sense or assert a homograph relationship before speaker review.
Existing ai is a draft with provisional copula analysis; do not link it from the recorded sentences until its relationship to the surface ai is confirmed.

Keep exact khadho and raja separate from existing khaadho and rajaa; these new entries are drafts for near-spelling review. Keep khade as a distinct draft until its relationship to khadho is confirmed.
Do not create independent headwords for dye, dhine, dhineese, dhya(n), dhinose or kayose. The attested giving forms are recorded under de; kayose is already recorded under kan.
Kapetho and kape(n) appear in cited desire examples, but a citation lemma and their distribution have not been established; do not generate a paradigm or new headwords from them.
Natho/nathi/nathaa are not a complete agreement paradigm; the feminine elicitation pair does not independently establish who gives or receives.
Nai is attested in both past giving and no-food contexts; nah is attested in commands and a future negative. Neither has an exclusive tense or sentence-type classification.
